picks.name: The Sustainability Buyer
picks.why_plausible: The brief targets sustainability-minded shoppers and this persona lists refillable_products and home_goods as affinities with sustainability as the core purchase driver. Price sensitivity medium fits a $35 mid-tier order.
lean_into: specific sustainability claims: concentrated refills replace single-use plastic bottles
honest performance claim: cleans as well as major brands
picks.ad_angle: Count the plastic bottles you stop buying — concrete, specific plastic reduction, not vague green talk.

picks.name: The Busy Parent
picks.why_plausible: Household and replenishment are top affinities and the brand sells recurring cleaning refills; the parent is time-poor and buys household staples in bulk. Mid price tier fits medium price sensitivity.
lean_into: stock up once, refills take less space than bottles
picks.ad_angle: One shelf of refills replaces a cabinet of bulky bottles — fewer restock runs for a busy household.

picks.name: The Value-Conscious Shopper
picks.why_plausible: Household and groceries affinities plus replenishment behavior match cleaning refills, and concentrates genuinely cost less per use since you stop repurchasing the bottle. High price sensitivity is served by the value_price signal in the brief.
lean_into: clear value props: you pay for cleaner, not water and plastic
picks.ad_angle: Concentrate math: stop paying to ship water and plastic — cost per bottle beats the big brands.

picks.name: The Convenience-First Millennial
picks.why_plausible: Replenishment plus household/convenience affinity fits a repeat-purchase cleaning refill, and refills ship small and light, which suits an urban apartment shopper. Medium price sensitivity fits the $35 order.
lean_into: lightweight refills that fit a small apartment
picks.ad_angle: Refills arrive in a padded envelope, not a heavy jug — the easiest way to restock in a city apartment.

plan.summary: The only strong match is Pantrygood's values-driven natural-grocery audience; Swiftcart is a direct cleaning-products competitor, most of the catalog is apparel, beauty or pet, so the plan is a single anchor test plus a small sustainability-led home test at Hearthstone Goods.

test.name: Pantrygood
test.adjustment_reason: Category scored 34 by treating this as groceries only, but the notes say shoppers are 'Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims' — the exact buying trigger for a plastic-free refill pitch.
test.rationale: Pantrygood is the clearest match in the catalog: values-driven natural-grocery buyers on a subscription/pantry replenishment cadence, and a $35 refill order is an easy add against an $86 typical basket.

evidence.quote: Values-driven shoppers. Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

test.risk: High-income West/Northeast buyers may already subscribe to an incumbent refill brand, so the offer must lead on performance parity, not novelty.

excluded.name: Swiftcart
excluded.rationale: Swiftcart sells cleaning_products itself, so it is a direct competitor and stays excluded despite 84M impressions.

excluded.name: Hearthstone Goods
excluded.adjustment_reason: Category scored 16 as cookware, but the notes read 'Sustainability-motivated kitchen buyers' with a 'non_toxic' subcategory and 'new-home life events' — the closest home-and-values intent in the catalog.
excluded.rationale: Hearthstone's buyers are sustainability-motivated and often setting up a new home, which is exactly when a refill system gets adopted; the tradeoff is only 2.8M impressions and a $198 typical basket.

evidence.quote: Sustainability-motivated kitchen buyers. Gifting and new-home life events drive purchase

excluded.risk: A $35 refill looks trivial next to a $198 cookware order, and low reach means slow learning.

excluded.name: Kitchenly
excluded.rationale: Kitchenly's family households buy on convenience, not values — the notes describe them as 'Convenience-motivated but food-interested', with no sustainability signal to hook a refill pitch.
excluded.risk: Meal-kit checkout attention is on tonight's dinner, not household restocking.

excluded.name: Daily Form
excluded.rationale: Daily Form's audience is 'skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims', so a 'cleans as well as major brands' claim needs proof, and 4.2M impressions cap the upside anyway.
excluded.risk: Unsubstantiated performance claims would be actively penalized by this audience.

excluded.name: Pop & Sip
excluded.rationale: Pop & Sip shoppers are 'Health-curious but indulgence-seeking' beverage buyers — adjacent on wellness values but with no household-supply intent at checkout.
excluded.risk: Indulgence mindset converts poorly to a chore-category refill purchase.

excluded.name: Studiogrid
excluded.rationale: Studiogrid users are booking fitness and spa appointments, a services context with no shared values tags and no link to restocking the cleaning cupboard.

evidence.quote: Appointment-based booking. Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness

excluded.name: Ruffco
excluded.rationale: Ruffco is off-category pet retail; big reach but shoppers here buy pet food, not household supplies.

excluded.name: Movewell
excluded.rationale: Movewell sells activewear to fitness-engaged shoppers with no sustainability or household signal in its notes.

excluded.name: Pawline
excluded.rationale: Pawline is off-category pet supplies, and its 4.8M impressions would not justify a test even if adjacency were stronger.

excluded.name: Cloudfoot
excluded.rationale: Cloudfoot's 'Comfort + sustainability messaging' matches the values story, but footwear is off-category so it stays excluded.

excluded.name: Tailcrate

campaign.name: Refillable, concentrated household cleaning products sold as refills to replace single-use plastic bottles · post-purchase launch

bid_strategy.rationale: $35 first order (assumed) × 0.30 = $10.50 target CPA: one-time purchase, so the first order has to pay back the acquisition. The max CPA allows headroom while the campaign learns over 14 days.

frequency_cap.rationale: Offers appear once, right after checkout; repeating them reads as spam.

experiment.graduate_rule: After 14 days, move a test publisher to core if its CPA is at or below target; cut any placement above max CPA.
experiment.notes: Creatives rotate evenly until each has enough conversions to compare.

assumptions: Assumed a mid-market price and about $35 first order since no pricing was given.
Assumed one-time purchases with repeat refills rather than a subscription.
Assumed a broad adult household audience, any gender.
Allowable CPA is 30% of first order value (one time); replace with real margin and LTV.
warnings: No publisher cleared the recommended bar, so the whole budget is a test. Treat results as exploratory.
Target CPA is based on an assumed order value. Confirm price before launch.
